question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(1\right)y=1,\quad y(0)=6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=1.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1y) & =e^{x}\cdot 1 \\ e^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{x}y & =e^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x}) & =e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int e^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{x} & =1\left(1 e^{x}\right)+C \\ ye^{x} & =e^{x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + e^{x}\right) e^{- x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(e^{(0)})+C}{(e^{(0)})} \\ 6 & =\frac{1+C}{1} \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=1 + 5 e^{- x}.
$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1y) & =e^{x}\cdot 2 \\ e^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{x}y & =2 e^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x}) & =2 e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2 e^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{x} & =2\left(1 e^{x}\right)+C \\ ye^{x} & =2 e^{x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 2 e^{x}\right) e^{- x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(2 e^{(0)})+C}{(e^{(0)})} \\ -1 & =\frac{2+C}{1} \\ C & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0,\,y(\frac{\pi }{2})=2
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y) & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ yx & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})=2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C}{(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\ 2 & =\frac{2C}{\pi } \\ C & =\pi\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\pi)}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi}{x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x} \\  & =\frac{- \cos{\left(x \right)} + \pi}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4 x^{2},\quad x>0,\quad y(1)=-5
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The first step is to write the equation in standard form,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =4 x^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}\left(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\right) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 4 x^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y & =4 x\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=4 x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & =x^{2}\cdot 4 x \\ x^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 xy & =4 x^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2}) & =4 x^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 4 x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ yx^{2} & =x^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{C + x^{4}}{x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=-5$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =\frac{((1)^{4})+C}{((1)^{2})} \\ -5 & =\frac{1+C}{1} \\ C & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{x^{4} - 6}{x^{2}}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(\frac{2}{x}\right)y=\frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x^{2}},\quad x>0,\quad y(\pi)=-5
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x^{2}}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & =x^{2}\cdot \frac{\cos{\left(x \right)}}{x^{2}} \\ x^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 xy & =\cos{\left(x \right)} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2}) & =\cos{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \cos{\left(x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ yx^{2} & =\sin{\left(x \right)}+C \\ y & =\frac{C + \sin{\left(x \right)}}{x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\pi)=-5$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi) & =\frac{(\sin{\left((\pi) \right)})+C}{((\pi)^{2})} \\ -5 & =\frac{0+C}{\pi^{2}} \\ C & =- 5 \pi^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{\sin{\left(x \right)} - 5 \pi^{2}}{x^{2}}.
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\sin{\left(x \right)}}{x}.$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)y=\frac{3 x}{2},\quad y(0)=-5
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{3 x}{2}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}y) & =e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\cdot \frac{3 x}{2} \\ e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}}{2}y & =\frac{3 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}) & =\frac{3 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{x^{2}}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}} & =\int 3e^u\,\text{d}u \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}} & =3e^u+C \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}} & =3 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 3 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{4}}\right) e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-5$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(3 e^{\frac{(0)^{2}}{4}})+C}{(e^{\frac{(0)^{2}}{4}})} \\ -5 & =\frac{3+C}{1} \\ C & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=3 - 8 e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{4}}.
$$
